item.title: Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada
item.description: Chef Soliat Bada Anyone who grew up in a Nigerian home knows the line. You suggest buying food outside, and before you finish the sentence, someone reminds you that there’s rice at home. It is usually the end of the conversation. In Asali Africa’s new series, it is where the conversation starts. There’s Rice at Home is a cooking and conversation show from Asali Africa, the Lagos-based creative development agency, hosted by Chef Soliat Bada . In each episode, Soliat cooks one rice dish with a guest, and while the pot does its work, the two get into the kind of talk that usually happens around food: family, money and what success really looks like. Rice is the most ordinary thing in a Nigerian kitchen, and the show makes a good case that it doesn’t have to taste ordinary. Over five episodes, released every two weeks, the menu travels from Jamaica to Saudi Arabia, back home to Nigeria and on to Louisiana. You don’t just watch the food get made, either. The recipes are written up in full on Asali Africa’s website, with the ingredients and method laid out step by step, so you can watch Soliat cook a dish and then make it in your own kitchen. The season opens with Rice and Peas with Oxtail, the Jamaican Sunday staple of rice cooked in coconut milk with red kidney beans (the “peas”), served beside rich, slow-cooked oxtail. Soliat’s guest is Michael Famoroti , co-founder of Stears, and their conversation turns to family and black tax: the expectation that once you start earning, you start supporting the people who raised you. Read the full recipe for Rice and Peas with Oxtail . Rice and peas with oxtail, from Episode 1 Soliat Bada and Michael Famoroti in Episode 1 Episode 2 moves to the Gulf for lamb kabsa, Saudi Arabia’s national dish, fragrant with dried lime and seven spice. Soliat is joined by Bella Adeleke , CEO of Asali Africa and founder of the fashion label Garbe, for a conversation about redefining success. Read the full recipe for Lamb Kabsa . Lamb kabsa, from Episode 2 Still to come are Nigerian fried rice with fried turkey and dodo, cooked with Toyin Jolapamo and Nneoma Mere; jambalaya with Goldie Iyamu and Vanessa Iloenyosi ; and a season finale with Edwin Okolo and Temi Omolehinwa. For more on Asali Africa and the products and ideas it develops, visit asali.africa . Episodes 1 and 2 are out now on YouTube. item.title: Beyond the Mini LED Label: What Should Define Good Mini LED Performance?
item.description: The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel. It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes. From Presence To Performance That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point. The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be. The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly. Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled? Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth. That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth. Market scale does not, on its own, define technology leadership. What it does provide is evidence that a manufacturer has become an important participant in how the category develops. For a company operating at that scale, leadership increasingly includes helping make the technology easier to understand and giving consumers clearer ways to evaluate what they are buying. Defining Category Leadership Category leadership in Mini LED should therefore be broader than shipment rankings. It can be understood through four connected areas: sustained market scale, continued investment in the fundamentals of backlight performan

item.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
item.description: The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics. The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution. Read more OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI. Advertisement “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis , but that stopped short of a full proof. Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages. Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt. However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.” A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now

item.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
item.description: null A snapshot of the Himalayas captured from aboard the ISS. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse. This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest. Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4Q November 17, 2026 Why is it incredible? From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission , even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range. It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home. Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

item.title: US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop
item.description: The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA's effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved. The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic. Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN . Bedford also said that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20. Read full article Comments

item.title: Lagos Hosts 2026 International Theatre Festival, Featuring Local and International Productions
item.description: The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival (LITF) has concluded successfully, attracting over 20,000 attendees from November 9 to 15, 2026. Featuring more than 25 productions, international performances from Kenya, Brazil, Norway and Canada, high-profile diplomatic engagements and a spectacular Opening Night Gala, the festival reinforced its growing position as an important platform for showcasing Nigerian creativity and connecting global theatre communities. The impressive turnout, diversity of productions and international participation demonstrated the growing appetite for live theatre and the potential of cultural platforms to stimulate creative enterprise, encourage international collaboration and strengthen Nigeria’s global cultural presence. A Vision For Global Recognition Speaking on the success of the festival, Founder and Creative Producer, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “Our ambition has always been to create more than a theatre festival. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and bringing international performers from four countries to Lagos is a powerful affirmation of this vision. Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence. The Stage Is Everywhere, and Africa must claim its rightful place on that stage.” A Week Of Culture And Collaboration The festival opened on November 9 with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrated chef Hilda Baci in a unique fusion of culinary artistry and live performance. The week also featured diplomatic and cultural engagements hosted by the United States Consul General in Lagos and the British Embassy, alongside a networking reception organised by the British Council for festival directors and participating production companies. These engagements highlighted the importance of international partnerships and cultural diplomacy in advancing Nigeria’s creative industry. A Celebration Of Excellence A major highlight was the Opening Night Gala, held on November 13 at Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, which welcomed over 1,000 guests, including the Governor of Lagos State, Babajide Olusola Sanwo-Olu ; the Chargé d’Affaires of the US Mission in Nigeria; the US Consul General; the British Deputy High Commissioner; the Consul General of Brazil; the Consul General of South Africa, the Ambassador of the Republic of Korea; alongside other members of the diplomatic corps, heads of institutions, government representatives, international delegates and leading figures in the creative industry. item.title: Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block said in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases. The report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S. Square sellers from Nov. 1, 2025, to Oct. 15, 2026. The median payment was about $13, and the average was about $29. Food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found. That is a bigger share than the category’s 67.5% slice of regular card payments on Square over the same period. “Most bitcoin payments are small and routine,” the company wrote on X Thursday, calling the report one of the first datasets on how people spend bitcoin in the local economy. Coffee, quick bites and repeat visits Coffee shops and fast food businesses accounted for 62.6% of the bitcoin payments in the food and drink category, with a median payment of $9.10. Grocery stores made up a smaller share but had the highest average payment in the group, at $60.73. Small tickets dominated. About 42% of bitcoin payments on Square were under $10, and 65.1% were under $20. Those sub-$20 payments made up just 19.1% of total payment value, though, with a few larger purchases accounting for much of the dollars spent. Customers also came back. Among Cash App users who paid with bitcoin at least twice at the same merchant, the median was three purchases per customer-merchant pair. About 44% of bitcoin payments from Cash App were repeat payments, and 86% of those came within 30 days. The activity was not limited to Block’s own app. External Lightning wallets such as Strike, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix and Coinbase handled 56.6% of Square bitcoin payments and about 66% of payment value, while Cash App wallets made up the rest. Square sellers can choose how much of each sale they keep in bitcoin, and Square converts the rest to dollars automatically. Block said zero-fee processing for bitcoin payments on Square has been extended through Dec. 31, 2027. Local governments are testing similar setups, with Miami-Dade County now taking bitcoin for property taxes and converting it to dollars. A push for a de minimis bitcoin exemption Block tied the data to tax policy. Under current U.S. federal rules, paying with bitcoin generally means calculating a capital gain or loss on every purchase, even a $10 coffee, the company said. A Morning Consult survey that Block commissioned found that 23.6% of businesses that don’t accept bitcoin cite tax and accounting complexity as a reason. That is about the same share that cite regulation, refunds or price swings. Among businesses that have considered taking bitcoin but haven’t, the figure was 27%. Consumers pointed to friction, too. Morning Consult surveyed 8,669 U.S. adults who are aware of bitcoin in August. Among those who don’t own it, 29.6% said they would

item.title: Microsoft's last non-security preview of 2026 packs a punch
item.description: Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview update of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for users who prefer darker rooms. The optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy. The big-ticket item is the "new Windows Search Experience." We saw a preview of this last month, and Microsoft has gone well beyond the "just make it work" request of many Windows users. Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search. We're less convinced by inline actions, which let users perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. In our testing, "turn on dark mode" worked, but "switch on dark mode" did not, thus highlighting the limitations of the tool. In addition, we remain unconvinced that Windows Search is the place to run actions. That said, anything that makes Windows Search less of a punchline for unkind jokes about performance and accuracy is welcome, as are other features, including an optional screen-brightening feature for Windows Hello facial recognition in dim rooms, and the PowerToys-esque Run dialog, which users can enable in Settings. While some of the new features won't be enabled immediately, Microsoft has included fixes that will be available right away. One addresses an issue where Windows Fax and Scan could fail to connect to a fax server. Handy for those occasions when email falls over into a heap . There are also fixes for Windows IoT Enterprise LTSC activation failures and the misleading "Something went wrong" message shown on Android devices during cross-device passkey authentication. At the time of writing, Microsoft still lists the problem as something for which "we are working on a resolution to be released in a future Windows update." Sadly, not everything has been pushed off the naughty step. SQL Server queries using OLE DB providers can still leave connections to external databases open after they've finished. Microsoft is working on that one and "will provide an update in an upcoming release." ®

item.title: Bitcoin Hovers Just Above Average Holder’s Cost Basis as Price Keeps Dipping
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Hovers Just Above Average Holder’s Cost Basis as Price Keeps Dipping Bitcoin is trading just above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network, and a break below that level would put the average holder at a loss for the first time since early 2023, Glassnode, an onchain analytics firm posted Friday. The price of bitcoin sat near $61,700 on Friday after sliding below $62,000. The realized price is a measure of what holders paid, not where the market trades. When bitcoin trades above it, the typical coin is sitting on a gain. Below it, the typical coin is underwater. The margin is thin. The firm said the MVRV ratio, which compares bitcoin’s market value with its realized value, sits “just above 1.” A reading of 1 means the market price has fallen all the way to the realized price. What the realized price measures Realized price values each coin at the price it last moved on the blockchain, then averages across the supply. Look Into Bitcoin describes it as bitcoin’s average cost basis. Because it tracks the price when coins last changed hands, it moves far more slowly than the market. The MVRV ratio expresses the same idea as a multiple. Above 1, holders are in profit on average. Below 1, they are not. A reading just above 1 means the market price is only a sliver higher than what the average coin cost. The firm did not give the exact realized price in its post, which included a chart. That leaves the exact cushion between today’s price and the average cost basis unstated. Bitcoin Magazine Pro’s full realized price chart sits behind a login, so the current level could not be confirmed independently for this report. “The average Bitcoin holder is still in profit,” the firm wrote. “The margin is thin.” Outflows and liquidations add to the pressure The slide has come with heavy selling from funds. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost about $541 million on Thursday, its largest one-day outflow since it launched in January 2024, Bloomberg reported . U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total that day. The selling stands out against the buying earlier in the fall. Institutions piled into bitcoin ETFs through the third quarter, pushing their combined holdings to a record, Bitcoin Magazine reported this week. Leveraged traders took losses too. More than $700 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, and about 86% of them were bets on higher prices. Bitcoin accounted for roughly $200 million of the total. CoinShares sees range trading through 2027 CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said the drop is part of a longer downturn rather than the start of a new one. “I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another,” he said in a note dated Nov. 18. item.title: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space
item.description: Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers. The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips. SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter. item.title: Bitcoin Price Slips Near $61,500 as Tech Selloff Spreads to Asia
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Slips Near $61,500 as Tech Selloff Spreads to Asia The bitcoin price slipped to near $61,500 on Friday morning, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a selloff in technology stocks that followed Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut spread to Asian markets and dragged bitcoin to its lowest level since July. Bitcoin first broke below $62,000 on Thursday evening, after Thursday afternoon’s report showed it giving back a rebound toward $64,000. The bitcoin price then slid to nearly $61,200 during Asian trading before bouncing back above $61,700. Friday marks a third straight day of losses. Asian stocks extend the AI rout The selling started in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi slid more than 5%, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics down around 6%. The Korea Exchange halted program selling for five minutes after the drop, while Japan’s Nikkei fell as much as 4.85% to a seven-month low. U.S. futures pointed lower too. Nasdaq-100 futures fell more than 1.7% and S&P 500 futures dropped 0.8%, Yahoo Finance reported. Gold futures lost 3%. The S&P 500 is pointing to a seventh straight daily decline, its longest losing streak since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Anthropic shares fell 8% in premarket trading after closing their first session at $97.17, up 17% from the $83 IPO price. Nvidia was down about 2.4% and AMD fell nearly 7%, CNBC reported. Hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials this week also weighed on sentiment, Reuters said. ETF outflows and liquidations pressure the bitcoin price Bitcoin funds are feeling the pressure. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $541.1 million in net outflows on Thursday, its largest single-day outflow since launch. That topped the previous record of $528.3 million set on Jan. 30. The fund bled $2 billion over nine straight days of outflows earlier this month. Leveraged traders took heavy losses as the bitcoin price broke support. Bitcoin liquidations hit $712.9 million over 24 hours, with $614 million coming from long positions. Open interest in bitcoin futures fell to $18 billion from $20 billion a week ago, and funding rates flipped broadly negative as traders unwound their bets. Traders are now watching whether the bitcoin price can hold the $60,000 area. A large pocket of long positions sits in the $60,500 to $60,900 band, just below the current price, and could come into play on a further drop. Bitcoin is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022. Crypto stocks slide before the bell Crypto stocks pointed lower in premarket trading. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $83.90, down about 2.6% from Thursday’s close of $86.13, after the stock fell for a sixth straight day on Thursday. Coinbase (COIN) slipped about 2.7% to near $106. item.title: Microsoft suggests Registry hack to work around hotpatch woes
item.description: Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it. Microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations. The November hotpatch is causing application errors, including in little-used and obscure apps such as Outlook. Affected applications may fail during installation, launch, or use, displaying errors such as " ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099) ." Microsoft's investigation points to applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, msi.dll. The problem is more common with 32-bit software, but can also affect 64-bit applications "under certain circumstances." The workaround involves fiddling with the Registry on affected devices, so is not for the faint of heart and a backup is a good idea before diving in. Microsoft says the key " HotPatchTableSize " in the folder " HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management " needs to be set to " 2000 " followed by a restart. Just the thing to round out the week for administrators. The issue affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security update. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft said. Windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration. "Hotpatch update package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft said, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency." The offending hotpatch, KB5132043 , was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline , which was a prerequisite. Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: " What could possibly go wrong? " Thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®

item.title: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone
item.description: Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation's most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX showed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we'll see you again the first week of December. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Europe's leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker . Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports . Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company's most recent fundraising round in June. Read full article Comments

item.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Future) Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close). Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare. item.title: AI could open wallets where ERP upgrade pitches can't, says PwC
item.description: Global consultancy PwC says IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch. The Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration. Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade. Thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP users last year found that 95 percent said building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging. Speaking to The Register , Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that. "Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case." SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has announced Fusion Claw . With both of these new technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems. "It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she said. An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. item.title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
item.description: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government. The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters. The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month. A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. item.description: It's now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I've known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It's no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today. So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I'd like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I'm unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars' future through your support will mean I don't have to. But I'd rather make a case for why you'll benefit from supporting Ars. item.title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
item.description: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Read full article Comments

item.title: Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in
item.description: A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2. The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again." Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored." Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID. Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected. An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets. Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057 , the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

item.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
item.description: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme Continue reading...

item.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
item.description: null An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all? Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. Lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data. That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein. Take it away Einstein Einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature. The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. Around this would be a spherical boundary at which not even light has the velocity needed to escape this region. Referred to as the Schwarzschild radius, that boundary became

item.title: SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule returns to Earth from the ISS
item.description: null SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth. The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov. 20) at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China. The freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at 5:03 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). The Dragon launched Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it was the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program. The capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15 , delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It brought a lot of stuff down to Earth, too. "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an update on Tuesday (Nov. 17). "The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth ," they added. Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight. Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking, then again at 8:55 p.m. ET on Nov. 21 with news of splashdown.

item.title: Ubuntu Core Desktop targets 28.04 debut, with default status in its sights
item.description: Canonical is targeting Ubuntu 28.04 LTS for the release of its immutable Core Desktop, with a stretch goal of making it the default download for Ubuntu 30.04. Canonical's VP of engineering, Jon Seager, set out the timetable in his opening keynote at Ubuntu Summit 26.10. Yes, we know, we have heard this before: we reported on his plans last month . But this time, there's the beginning of a release schedule. Seager said that Ubuntu Core is already out there in tens of thousands of IoT devices – which seems like a modest estimate to us, and to him too, as he quickly added "maybe more." Despite some noise a few years ago, though, what's still missing is the desktop version. Seager's slides listed three bullet points: that Core Desktop will be "immutable," "composable," and "attestable." As he put it, they are "taking the whole of the Linux operating system, and cramming the whole thing into snaps." Acknowledging that this is going to be wildly controversial, he said: "This is one for the Redditors." He's right. There is a lot of resistance to snap, and in direct response, advocacy of the Red Hat-backed Flatpak instead – but we have seen almost none that is based on either system's technical merits. Much of that opposition concerns claims of one being more open than the other. We've looked at how both systems work, and our impression is that the implementation of snap is cleaner, simpler, easier to use, and more comprehensible. Snap does depend on systemd, which Flatpak does not – but only for now. Flatpak NG is in development and will also need everyone's favorite init system. Ubuntu Core's immutability is not new technology: even Core 16 is now a decade old. It has supported in-place version upgrades since Core 22. We have reported before that Canonical remains strongly committed to its packaging format, and that commitment seems stronger than ever. Seager continued: "Never has a model like snap confinement been more relevant… we're finally in a position where we can bring this to the desktop." The core idea of an immutable OS is that "much more of the system is not writable at runtime," meaning that it "can't be messed with once the system has booted." He talked about the same three use cases we discussed last month. The "browser-centric machine" is the company's analog to Google ChromeOS, and he said that it's essentially ready now, suggesting that everyone listening probably has a family member whose computer is basically just a way to use a web browser. The second was the dedicated games machine, which we interpret as a response to Valve's SteamOS. This edition, he said, would "boot straight to Steam," with "just enough of a shell to launch games." There's also an immutable "development workstation," and here, he offered the example of developers who need to work on some long-unsupported hardware or software, for whom an immutable OS means that you "can't brick your system by installing some weird old dependencies, unmaintained for 20 years." item.title: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
item.description: Artist’s impression of BepiColombo orbiting Mercury ESA/ATG medialab After a long and ponderous journey, the BepiColombo spacecraft will finally enter Mercury’s orbit on 21 November. Over the course of the next year, it will investigate the planet’s geology, its tenuous atmosphere and its magnetic field in an effort to understand how it formed and evolved over time. BepiColombo , a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), launched in October 2018. Mercury’s proximity to the sun makes it incredibly difficult to reach without overshooting the planet and falling into the sun, so the spacecraft had to take a long and looping path over the past eight years, flying past both Venus and Mercury several times and using their gravity to make subtle tweaks to its trajectory. In 2024, an issue with the thrusters lengthened that journey even further, pushing the arrival date back from 2025 to 2026. Now, it has finally arrived. Read more 6 of the most fascinating moments in the life of our solar system While it is arriving at Mercury as a single spacecraft, BepiColombo actually comprises two separate orbiters: ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO, or Mio). In December, the two will split apart and move to different orbits – MPO on a near-circular path that takes 2.3 hours to complete an orbit, and Mio on a more distant elliptical orbit, where it will take 9.3 hours to circle Mercury. Advertisement Those split orbits complement the differing scientific objectives of the two spacecraft. MPO is more than twice the size of MMO, and its 11 scientific instruments focus largely on studying Mercury itself . Its instruments include several types of spectrometer to measure the makeup of the surface, a laser altimeter to map its terrain and instruments to study the makeup of Mercury’s extremely thin atmosphere, called an exosphere. Mio’s more distant orbit will allow it to study a broader area around Mercury. It has five sets of scientific instruments to study the magnetic field and atmosphere of the planet, as well as the solar wind that blows strongly in the area close to the sun. Free newsletter Sign up to Launchpad Sign up to newsletter Now that the BepiColombo spacecraft are entering orbit, their primary mission is expected to last only one Earth year, which is a little more than four Mercury years. The mission could potentially be extended for another year, but beyond that the combination of limited fuel and extreme temperatures will make it all but impossible to keep going. Over the course of the year, researchers hope that BepiColombo will provide enough data to solve some of Mercury’s many mysteries. Mercury’s magnetic field is bewildering, because it originates 400 kilometres above the planet’s centre and should have faded away long ago. Its atmosphere must be continuously supplied with material from the surface, but we are unsure exactly how that occurs.

item.title: Support tech fixed malware by charging client less for their services
item.description: Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call , The Register 's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city. "I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends." The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits. Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC. "I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time. "He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'." Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself! "It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product." So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers. Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact. "I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!" Have you done less tech support to deliver more value? If so, click here to send On Call an email and charge us with the responsibility of telling your story on a future Friday. ®

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 20 – V-G-R
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. V-G-R Explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory are read V-G-R. That’s a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft currently in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away. How long did it take the message to reach humanity’s most distant interstellar spacecraft ? Traveling at the speed of light, the answer is one day . In fact, the Voyager 1 spacecraft was confirmed to reach its one light-day distance milestone on November 18, at 10:16:07 UTC, nearly 50 years after launch in 1977. For extra credit, fans of math can calculate that at one light-day per 50 years, Voyager 1 will reach its one light-year (365 light-days) distance milestone in about 18,250 years. item.title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Stormy Southwest Pacific Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific. On November 15, 2026 , the Fiji Meteorological Service began issuing updates about a slow-moving tropical disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands. Within just a few days, it had become one of the most intense November tropical cyclones the region has seen in decades. Named Xavier , the system intensified rapidly , thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones . Xavier was the basin’s second named storm of the season, following only Wati , a short-lived storm that emerged in October. As Xavier developed, NASA satellite data showed the storm churning along the southwestern edge of a massive tongue of warm water spanning from the west coast of South America to the central Pacific—a telltale sign of the El Niño that has been present in the region since June . When the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this image at 02:53 Universal Time on November 17, 2026 (4:53 p.m. Cook Islands Time on November 16), forecasters estimated Xavier had maximum winds of about 195 kilometers (120 miles) per hour. Winds reached a peak intensity of 220 kilometers (140 miles) per hour later that day, a Category 5 storm on the cyclone intensity scale used in the region or a Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale . The storm ranks as the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the international date line on record, noted Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach . Xavier’s formation east of the date line, near the northern Cook Islands, was unusual, but its easterly position aligns with research that indicates that storm activity in the region typically shifts northeast during El Niño years. Research also shows that El Niño tends to fuel storms that strengthen at an unusually rapid pace . According to news reports, Xavier damaged homes and caused power disruptions as it passed the northern Cook Islands. It then encountered dry air and a less favorable wind shear environment and slowly weakened as it pushed westward, reducing the threat that it posed to Samoa and American Samoa. Xavier is likely one of the first of several storms to affect the region in the coming months. A seasonal outlook from the Fiji Meteorological Se

item.title: From Dancehall to Rumba, Rema Stretches His Sound on New EP “E-Mortal Boy (EMB)” | Listen
item.description: Rema releases his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB), featuring Wizkid, Theodora, BNYX, and Kah-Lo. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram For weeks, Rema has been teasing us with a new project—first came “ TEA ” and then “ Oh No “, and if you have had those on repeat on your playlist, you now have the entire package with his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy ( EMB ). Ever since his self-titled debut EP in 2019, the Benin-born star has never been interested in staying boxed into one sound. Following his 2023 EP Ravage and his 2024 Grammy-nominated album HEIS , he uses this new seven-song collection to pull rhythms from across the Black diaspora into one bold, genre-hopping ride. If you already had “TEA” on loop when its dancehall bounce, glossy pop, and techno twists took over the Nigerian timeline, or kept “Oh No” close for that percussion-heavy Rvssian groove about a lover’s mixed signals, they both sit right inside the full lineup alongside five more records . The biggest headline moment opens the project: “ Feel Alright ” pairs Rema with Wizkid for their very first official joint release, a smooth ballad about satisfying a lover’s appetite. From there, he switches gears across “ Velvet “, where rumba drums meet slick guitar riffs as he vows to take on the world for someone special, and “ TANZANIA “, a BNYX-assisted track with Bollywood score-inspired flair. The rest of the EP keeps that same adventurous streak alive. On “ SUGA “, Rema teams up with French Congolese singer Theodora for a rougher, grunge-leaning sound, before closing out on “ Bang Bang ” with longtime collaborator London and Nigerian dance music favourite Kah-Lo . Nearly a decade into his run, Rema still sounds completely locked in on what comes next, leaving you with seven quick tracks to drop straight into your weekend rotation. item.title: Big Tech's compliance with EU market rules is performative, consumer group says
item.description: Big Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which says the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice. BEUC said : "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products." The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023 , imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition. The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on. BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026. In the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine. "Microsoft also regularly prompts users who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC said. Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store users to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications. The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge users into handing over their data. item.title: US let Nvidia and AMD sell bucketloads of chips to military-linked Chinese companies
item.description: The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military. That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast (R-FL), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China. The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items. BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance. But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent. Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies , the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security. Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft. Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons. A diverting drama The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The New York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation. Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law. One of the documents Mast shared says “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.” Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk. Earlier this week, Washington adopted a new policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions. item.title: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else
item.description: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP , Java , and PostgreSQL , VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories. VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890 , a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. VMware also wants its users to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root. The prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software. The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010 , which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618). VMware plans to ship new versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol. A KVM curiosity Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours. This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312 , a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host. It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses. This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5. Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Terra Security says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs. Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17 th . The CVE then appeared on November 18. Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours. item.title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way
item.description: The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023. "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch ," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them." Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime. "At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption." Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering. Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained. Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network. "Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life." At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play. Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content." Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements. "I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and w
